q: BM25 (sparse) and dense retrieval (embeddings) win on different query types. Name a query where BM25 wins, a query where dense wins, and explain *why* hybrid (RRF) usually beats either alone.
answer_outline: BM25 wins on exact-term queries — 'What is BM25?' returns the BM25 doc top-1 because the rare token 'BM25' has high IDF weight. Dense wins on synonym/paraphrase queries — 'machines agreeing on a value despite failures' finds the Raft and Paxos docs even though those words aren't in the query, because the embedding captures semantic similarity. Hybrid via RRF wins because the two retrievers fail in *different* ways: BM25 fails on synonyms but ranks exact terms confidently; dense fails on rare exact terms (which get diluted in the embedding) but handles paraphrases. RRF fuses by reciprocal rank, so a doc that's #1 in either ranking gets a high score, and the union of strengths covers more query types than either alone. The cost is two indexes and two queries per request — usually worth it.

q: Cross-encoder reranking improves precision but adds latency. Walk through the pattern: why over-fetch with a cheap retriever, then rerank?
answer_outline: Cross-encoders score (query, doc) pairs by running the LLM-style transformer on each pair — accurate but O(query_doc_pairs) at query time. Running it over a 10M-doc corpus is impossibly expensive. Bi-encoders (your dense retriever) embed query and docs separately and compare with cosine — cheap, runs in milliseconds over millions of docs, but less accurate. The pattern: use the bi-encoder (cheap, lossy) to retrieve the top-K candidates (e.g. K=20-100), then run the cross-encoder (expensive, accurate) only on those K to re-order. You spend 50-200ms reranking 20 candidates instead of hours scoring all 10M. The same logical pattern shows up everywhere — coarse-then-fine, candidate-generation-then-scoring — it's how production search engines (and recommender systems) work.

q: In 2026, with Gemini 1.5 Pro's 2M context window, the threshold for RAG-vs-long-context has moved. When does RAG still earn its keep?
answer_outline: Three cases. (1) Corpus too large to fit even a 2M context: very large knowledge bases, every document on the internet, etc. (2) Corpus updates frequently and retrieval is cheaper than re-prompting: re-embed only the changed docs (one embedding call) vs sending the full corpus on every query (1.9M tokens × every query). (3) Cost-sensitive workloads: input tokens are billed; sending 5 retrieved docs per query (a few thousand tokens) costs a small fraction of sending the full corpus. Conversely, long-context wins on: small corpora (<50K tokens), high-quality use cases where you can't risk a retrieval miss, prototyping (zero infra), and tasks where the model needs to reason over the *full* corpus rather than over a retrieved subset (some legal, multi-document QA tasks). The threshold has moved from 'always RAG above 4K tokens' to something like 'long-context up to ~100K tokens; RAG above'. Decide by measurement on your actual task, not by industry default.
